A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same discrepancy-minimization work and provide readable text, equations, algorithms, figures, and tables. The technical sections of v1 can be matched to Appendices A–I of v2; Appendix J adds experiments.

before.justification: v1 contains theoretical algorithms, proofs, illustrative diagrams, and an asymptotic runtime comparison, but no original experimental or simulation results.

after.justification: Appendix J and Tables 2–4 report original experiments comparing objective values and runtimes with Larsen’s algorithm on three synthetic matrix families.

M1.justification: The matched pseudocode retains the same hereditary projection, implicit leverage-score sampling, boundary search, partial coloring, and lazy-update procedures. The corrected leverage-score definition does not change the existing QR-based computation.

E1.justification: v2 introduces empirical evaluation on uniformly sampled sign matrices, 2D corner matrices, and 2D halfspace matrices. v1 evaluates no datasets or synthetic matrix instances experimentally.

E2.justification: Larsen’s algorithm becomes an experimentally evaluated baseline throughout Tables 2–4, establishing an empirical comparison absent from v1. The earlier theoretical comparator set in Table 1 is retained.

E3.justification: The new experiments report objective values and runtimes for 400×400, 2000×2000, and 10000×1000 matrices at reported sparsity values 1.0, 0.5, and 0.1. Appendix J specifies that evaluation focuses on fast hereditary projection and excludes practical evaluation of the FMM-oriented lazy-update scheme.

E4.justification: Tables 2–4 add limited sensitivity evidence across matrix sizes, aspect ratios, and sparsity levels, including square-versus-tall comparisons relevant to the claimed advantage of sketching. No dedicated component-removal ablation or robustness study is added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports empirical run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new tables provide point results without uncertainty estimates; theoretical success probabilities are separate from empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 add 27 comparison rows, generally showing lower runtime with higher discrepancy objectives. For example, Table 2’s 10000×1000 uniform matrix at sparsity 1.0 reports runtime 63 versus Larsen’s 378, with objectives 140 versus 132. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 measurements.

T1.justification: Local revisions correct the Gaussian tail event, insert the missing inverse in the leverage-score definition, remove binary-only restrictions from discrepancy definitions, and adjust partial-coloring and runtime parameter domains. The main proof framework remains. Theorem C.2 also changes the stated per-call orthogonalization cost from O(n²) to O(n) without a corresponding algorithmic change or explanation.

C1.justification: The main claims retain the same hereditary-discrepancy approximation guarantee and runtimes: approximately nnz(A)+n³ combinatorially and nnz(A)+n^2.53 using fast matrix multiplication. The new conclusion restates these contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix J adds a practical limitation: large FMM constants motivate evaluating only the hereditary-projection improvement. It also interprets the experiments as a runtime–objective tradeoff and explains why larger gains are expected for tall matrices. These qualifications are absent from v1.

D1.justification: Appendix J supplies synthetic-data construction recipes, including unit-square point sampling, dominance tests, and halfspace generation. Existing algorithmic parameters are retained. Hardware, software, sparsification details, and implementation access are not supplied for the new experiments.

R1.justification: The new Related Work section substantially expands coverage of algorithmic discrepancy and sketching. v2 discusses Jambulapati–Reis–Tian’s bounded-entry results, updates matrix-multiplication references, and connects its data structure to lookahead algorithms through BNS19. Eldan–Singh remains the same cited work under the updated ES18 label.

P1.justification: v2 reorganizes the extensive technical development into Appendices A–I, adds Related Work and Conclusion sections, and rewrites portions of the abstract, introduction, and overview. Supporting subroutines are separated and reordered; author and affiliation information also changes.

P2.justification: All seven illustrations are retained, but several are relocated, resized, or rearranged. The row-selection diagrams move into the overview, and Figure 3 changes from vertically stacked to side-by-side panels. Table 1 adds a separate combinatorial-runtime row, and three experimental tables are introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful practical evidence about the runtime–discrepancy tradeoff, corrects several mathematical statements, and improves organization and research context. These provide a modest overall gain. The experiments remain limited by missing implementation and uncertainty information and do not validate the FMM/lazy-update component. The unexplained orthogonalization-cost revision also leaves the runtime justification unresolved, limiting the improvement in theoretical reliability.
